comparison: Both strongly support the technical specifications and system design of OT-TP-LSM (C3-C6, C31-C42, C44-C45). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation while peer reviewers acknowledge this as 'the first system of integrating the two' and confirm the technical implementation without challenge. Peer R1 also includes characterization claims (C46-C48) that OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

Both support the system characterization methodology (C46-C49). OpenEval validates the use of fluorescent microspheres and measured performance metrics. Peer reviewers accept the technical specifications including resolution measurements, with Reviewer 2 confirming 'high-speed and high-depth imaging' with stated specifications.

Both support the imaging depth comparison between OT-TP-LSM and 1PLSM (C50-C52). OpenEval emphasizes the three-fold improvement with specific measurements and acknowledges limitations. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly highlights 'better imaging depth than a single-photon excitation OT-LSM' as a key strength. Peer R2 also addresses PI depth enhancement (C72-C74) and tissue-specific depths (C8, C119) that OpenEval covers in separate results.

Both support the skin cancer imaging results (C55-C71, C142). OpenEval provides detailed validation through H&E histology correlation and emphasizes 3D visualization advantages. Peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique investigating various human cancer cells' with Reviewer 2 confirming successful 3D visualization across tissue types including skin.

Both support pancreatic tissue imaging with PI optimization (C72-C88). OpenEval validates quantitative depth improvements and H&E correlation. Peer reviewers confirm successful '3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate' and Reviewer 1 notes 'Use of propidium iodide (PI) provided a deeper imaging depth' as a strength.

Both support PDAC characterization (C89-C97, C143). OpenEval details the distinction between nonneoplastic and cancer structures with H&E validation. Peer reviewers encompass this within their confirmation of successful cancer cell visualization across tissue types and acceptance of 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness of this technique.'

Both support prostate tissue imaging distinguishing benign from malignant regions (C98-C105). OpenEval validates histological feature descriptions and equivalence to H&E. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms '3D visualization of human cancer cells in the skin, pancreas, and prostate' with no challenges to the prostate characterization.

Both support the CycleGAN implementation for virtual H&E generation (C107-C114, C125). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation with acknowledged limitations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this component through overall endorsement of the work as 'important' and providing 'convincing evidence,' with no criticism of the transparent acknowledgment of transformation limitations.

Both support the identification of CycleGAN limitations and future work needs (C126-C127). OpenEval frames these as reasonable assessments given observed issues. Peer reviewers accept the transparent presentation of limitations without criticism, suggesting agreement that this is appropriate for a proof-of-concept demonstration.

Both support tissue-specific imaging depth measurements and comparisons (C119-C122). OpenEval provides detailed mechanistic explanations for tissue-dependent variations. Peer reviewers confirm 'high-depth imaging' achievement and accept the comparative limitations versus conventional TPM as technical realities rather than fundamental flaws.

Both support the identification of aberration issues and proposed solutions (C128-C130). OpenEval validates this as appropriate critical self-assessment consistent with measured resolution. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly identifies 'Use of liquid prism to minimize the aberration induced by index mismatching' as 'interesting and potentially helpful,' accepting the technical trade-off.

Both support the acknowledgment of processing time limitations and proposed solutions (C135-C139, with OpenEval also covering C157-C161). OpenEval provides specific quantitative measurements and technical solutions. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through lack of criticism, viewing it as an addressable technical challenge rather than fundamental flaw.

Both support the background context and clinical potential (C1-C2, C12-C30 for OpenEval; C1, C12, C144 for peer). OpenEval validates the literature-supported rationale. Peer reviewers endorse the work as 'important' for 'lesser invasive evaluation of intraoperative 3D pathology' with 'broad interest to biologists and pathologists.'

Both support the demonstrated capabilities across tissue types (C115-C118, C140-C141, C144). OpenEval summarizes extensive imaging results with speculative attribution to Bessel beam technology. Peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence for the effectiveness' across multiple cancer types, confirming the broad applicability claims.

Both support the mechanistic advantages of two-photon excitation (C8-C9, C106). OpenEval validates imaging depths and addresses pathologist familiarity concerns. Peer Reviewer 1 highlights the integration providing 'better imaging depth' as a key strength, confirming the fundamental advantage of the approach.

OpenEval identifies a design trade-off between SHG collection efficiency and imaging depth (C133-C134) with suggestions for improvement. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this specific technical limitation.

OpenEval validates ethical approvals, compliance, and sample preparation protocols (C148-C156) as appropriate for reproducibility and research conduct. Peer reviewers do not explicitly comment on these methodological details.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the proposed improvements for adaptive optics and structured illumination (C123-C124, C131), noting these are speculative future work without experimental validation. Peer reviewers do not explicitly address these specific future directions.
